# Amazon EC2: questions

## Worked examples

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q015 -->
### Question 1

A company runs a legacy application on one Amazon EC2 instance. The instance is backed by Amazon EBS and uses an x86 instance type. The application cannot run on more than one instance at a time, and it now needs twice its current memory. The company has a 30-minute maintenance window tonight and wants minimal downtime. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- During the window, change the instance type of the running instance to a larger memory optimized x86 type without stopping it.
- During the window, hibernate the instance, change its instance type to a larger memory optimized x86 type, and then resume it.
- Create an AMI of the instance, launch a larger memory optimized x86 instance from the AMI, and point the clients to it.
- During the window, stop the instance, change its instance type to a larger memory optimized x86 type, and start it again.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** During the window, stop the instance, change its instance type to a larger memory optimized x86 type, and start it again.

**Deciding phrases.** "cannot run on more than one instance", "backed by Amazon EBS", "30-minute maintenance window", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the solution with the LEAST operational overhead that still keeps the downtime minimal.
2. I mark the constraints: one EBS-backed x86 instance, the application cannot run on two instances, it needs twice the memory, and the maintenance window is 30 minutes tonight.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict that I change the instance type while the instance runs, because that seems to give zero downtime.
4. I remove the AMI and new instance option, because it works but adds an image, a launch and a client change. I remove the hibernation option, because a hibernated instance cannot be modified.
5. Between the change while running and the stop, change and start, the difference is the stop. My first idea breaks because I must stop an EBS-backed instance before I can change its instance type. The stem gives a maintenance window, so a short stop is acceptable.
6. Check: stop, change to a larger memory optimized x86 type, and start again meets every constraint and keeps the same processor architecture. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** Scaling up needs a stop. [You must stop your instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance) [before you can change its instance type](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance), so you [plan for downtime](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance) inside the window. The new type keeps [the same processor architecture](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-same-processor-architecture), because the AMI of the instance is built for x86.

**Why not.**

- "During the window, change the instance type of ...": [You must stop your instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance) [before you can change its instance type](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-resize-must-stop-instance), so a running instance keeps its current type.
- "During the window, hibernate the instance, change its ...": After an [instance is hibernated, you can't modify it](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-hibernate-cannot-modify-while-hibernated), so the type change fails.
- "Create an AMI of the instance, launch a ...": A new instance from an AMI works, but it adds an image, a launch and a client change, which is more work than a stop and a type change.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the application can run on several instances behind a load balancer" instead: add instances, because horizontal scaling means [adding more instances to handle the load](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-vertical-vs-horizontal-definition).

**Takeaway.** Changing an instance type needs a stop, so plan the stop inside a maintenance window.

**Review.** [Scaling up needs a stop and scaling out adds instances instead](2-deep.md#scaling-up-needs-a-stop-and-scaling-out-adds-instances-instead-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 2

A company runs an internal web application on one large general purpose Amazon EC2 instance. Over the last month, average CPU utilization was 9%. The load is spiky: on weekday mornings, short peaks reach 85% CPU for about 15 minutes, and then the load falls again. Memory use stays low all day. The company wants to reduce cost and still serve the morning peaks without slow responses. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Move the application to a smaller general purpose instance with enough vCPUs for the 9% average CPU utilization of the last month.
- Move the application to a larger compute optimized instance, so that the short morning peaks use a smaller share of its available CPU.
- Move the application to a memory optimized instance of a smaller size, because low CPU use shows that memory limits the application.
- Move the application to a burstable T instance with the same vCPU count, so that idle hours earn CPU credits for the peaks.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Move the application to a burstable T instance with the same vCPU count, so that idle hours earn CPU credits for the peaks.

**Deciding phrases.** "average CPU utilization was 9%", "short peaks reach 85% CPU", "Memory use stays low", "MOST cost-effective"

**Think aloud.**

1. I read the last sentence first: it asks for the change that is the MOST cost-effective way to meet the requirements.
2. I mark the constraints: average CPU utilization is 9%, short morning peaks reach 85%, memory use stays low, and the peaks must not slow down.
3. Before I look at the options, I predict a burstable T instance, because a low average with short peaks is the pattern that CPU credits are made for.
4. I remove the memory optimized instance, because memory is not the limit. I remove the smaller general purpose instance, because a size for the 9% average has no room for the 85% peaks.
5. Between the burstable T instance and the larger compute optimized instance the difference is cost; the stem says the peaks are short and the average is low, so the T instance earns credits in idle hours and spends them in the peaks, and the larger instance pays for idle CPU.
6. Check: the burstable T instance keeps the same vCPU count, serves the peaks with credits, and costs less than the large fixed instance. Time: 90 seconds.

**Why.** A low average with short peaks is the burstable pattern. When CPU use is low, a fixed instance pays for idle cycles, and AWS points to [the low-cost burstable general purpose instances](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-low-utilization-waste-use-t). The T instance banks credits in quiet hours and spends them in the peaks.

**Why not.**

- "Move the application to a smaller general purpose ...": A size for the 9% average has no headroom for the 85% peaks, so responses slow down, and such a type [does not meet the performance requirements](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-optimizer-under-provisioned-definition).
- "Move the application to a larger compute optimized ...": It serves the peaks, but a larger instance pays for even more idle CPU, and [the low-cost burstable general purpose instances](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-low-utilization-waste-use-t) fit a low average better.
- "Move the application to a memory optimized instance ...": Memory use is low, so this family solves a problem that the stem does not have: it is built to [process large data sets in memory](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-memory-optimized).

**Twin.** If the stem said "CPU stays near 80% all day" instead: an M or C instance, because AWS suggests them when workloads [consistently require CPU usage much higher](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-burstable-sustained-high-cpu-use-m-or-c) than the baseline.

**Takeaway.** A low average with short CPU peaks fits a burstable T instance; steady high CPU fits M or C.

**Review.** [A burstable instance earns CPU credits while idle and spends them in peaks](2-deep.md#a-burstable-instance-earns-cpu-credits-while-idle-and-spends-them-in-peaks-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 3

A company plans to launch six Amazon EC2 instances of one instance type in a single Availability Zone for a new application. The instances will be launched together from one launch template, and the application team manages them. The instances exchange data constantly, and the application needs low latency and high throughput between them. Which placement approach for the instances will meet these requirements?

- Launch all six instances into a cluster placement group in the Availability Zone.
- Launch all six instances into a spread placement group in the Availability Zone.
- Launch the instances into a partition placement group with two partitions of three instances each.
- Launch the instances without a placement group, and let Amazon EC2 spread them across the underlying hardware.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Launch all six instances into a cluster placement group in the Availability Zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "exchange data constantly", "low latency and high throughput between them"

**Why.** Traffic between the instances decides this question. A cluster placement group places the instances close together for [low network latency, high network throughput, or both](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances). A cluster placement group [can't span multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-single-az), which fits six instances in a single zone.

**Why not.**

- "Launch all six instances into a spread placement ...": A spread placement group keeps the instances [each placed on distinct hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-critical-instances), which protects against shared failures but does not bring them closer together.
- "Launch the instances into a partition placement group ...": Each partition [has its own set of racks](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-partition-separate-racks) to [isolate the impact of hardware failure](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-partition-separate-racks), not to bring the instances close together.
- "Launch the instances without a placement group, and ...": Without a group, Amazon EC2 keeps instances [spread out across the underlying hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-optional-default-spread-out) to limit correlated failures, which works against low latency between them.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The instances are mission-critical, and one hardware failure must not affect more than one of them" instead: a spread placement group, with instances [each placed on distinct hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-critical-instances).

**Takeaway.** Traffic between the instances means a cluster placement group; separate hardware for a few critical instances means a spread placement group.

**Review.** [A placement group decides whether instances sit close together or apart](2-deep.md#a-placement-group-decides-whether-instances-sit-close-together-or-apart-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 4

A company runs a licensed application on one Amazon EC2 instance in a private subnet. Partner systems allow-list the private IP address of the application, and the software license is bound to the MAC address that the application uses. A hot standby instance with the same software runs in the same Availability Zone. If the primary instance fails, traffic must move to the standby with minimal downtime and without DNS or route table changes. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Give the application its address on a secondary network interface, and attach that interface to a standby instance in another Availability Zone after a failure.
- Detach the primary network interface from the failed instance, and attach it to the standby instance so that its addresses and MAC address move.
- Give the application its address on a secondary network interface, and attach that interface to the standby instance in the same zone after a failure.
- Launch a replacement instance from a recent AMI after a failure, assign it the same private IP address, and register its new MAC address with the vendor.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Give the application its address on a secondary network interface, and attach that interface to the standby instance in the same zone after a failure.

**Deciding phrases.** "allow-list the private IP address", "bound to the MAC address", "without DNS or route table changes", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** The addresses and the MAC address have to move without DNS changes, and a secondary network interface does that. [The attributes of a network interface follow it](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az) to the new instance, and [network traffic is redirected](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az). The move works because the standby is [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az).

**Why not.**

- "Give the application its address on a secondary ...": A network interface attaches to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az), so it cannot move to a standby in another zone.
- "Detach the primary network interface from the failed ...": [You can't detach a primary network interface](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-primary-cannot-detach), so the addresses on the primary interface stay with the failed instance.
- "Launch a replacement instance from a recent AMI ...": A new launch works, but each failure then needs an image, a launch and a license change, which is more downtime and more work than moving an interface.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the standby instance runs in another Availability Zone" instead: moving the interface fails, because a network interface attaches to instances [in the same Availability Zone](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eni-attributes-follow-same-az).

**Takeaway.** To fail over at the same private IP address and MAC address, move a secondary network interface to a standby in the same zone.

**Review.** [Recovery and a moved network interface keep an instances addresses after a failure](2-deep.md#recovery-and-a-moved-network-interface-keep-an-instances-addresses-after-a-failure-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 5

A company runs an analytics service on Amazon EC2 general purpose instances. The service loads a large data set into memory and runs queries against it. During busy periods, the service runs out of memory and slows down, but CPU utilization stays below 30%. Disk activity on the instances is low. The company wants to change the instance family without changing the application. Which instance family meets these requirements?

- Compute optimized instances, such as the C family, with more vCPUs for each instance
- Burstable performance instances, such as the T family, that earn credits for the busy periods
- Storage optimized instances, such as the I family, with fast local storage for the data set
- Memory optimized instances, such as the R family, with enough memory for the data set

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Memory optimized instances, such as the R family, with enough memory for the data set

**Deciding phrases.** "runs out of memory", "CPU utilization stays below 30%", "Disk activity on the instances is low"

**Why.** Find the resource that runs out. Here it is memory, and CPU and disk stay low. Memory optimized instances are built for workloads that [process large data sets in memory](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-memory-optimized). In an instance type name, the letter R stands for [memory optimized](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-instance-type-series-letters).

**Why not.**

- "Compute optimized instances, such as the C family, ...": Compute optimized instances serve [compute intensive applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-compute-optimized), and CPU stays low here, so more vCPUs do not fix the memory shortage.
- "Burstable performance instances, such as the T family, ...": A burstable instance [spends credits when it bursts above the baseline](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-earn-spend-credits) of CPU, and CPU credits add no memory.
- "Storage optimized instances, such as the I family, ...": Storage optimized instances serve [very large data sets on local storage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-storage-optimized) with heavy disk access, and disk activity here is low.

**Twin.** If the stem said "CPU utilization stays above 90% and memory use is low" instead: compute optimized instances, because they serve [compute intensive applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-family-compute-optimized).

**Takeaway.** Match the instance family to the resource that runs out: memory points to R, CPU to C, local disk to I.

**Review.** [The instance family matches the resource that limits your workload](2-deep.md#the-instance-family-matches-the-resource-that-limits-your-workload-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 6

A company plans to launch six Amazon EC2 instances of one instance type in a single Availability Zone for a new application. The instances will be launched together from one launch template, and the application team manages them. The instances are mission-critical, and one hardware failure must not affect more than one of them. Which placement approach for the instances will meet these requirements?

- Launch all six instances into a cluster placement group in the Availability Zone.
- Launch all six instances into a spread placement group in the Availability Zone.
- Launch the instances into a partition placement group with two partitions of three instances each.
- Launch the instances without a placement group, and let Amazon EC2 spread them across the underlying hardware.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Launch all six instances into a spread placement group in the Availability Zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "mission-critical", "one hardware failure must not affect more than one of them"

**Why.** The phrase about one hardware failure decides it. A spread placement group is for [a small number of critical instances](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-critical-instances), each on its own hardware. It supports [seven running instances in each Availability Zone](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-spread-max-7-running-per-az), so six instances fit in one zone.

**Why not.**

- "Launch all six instances into a cluster placement ...": A cluster placement group packs the instances close together for [low network latency, high network throughput, or both](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances), so one hardware failure can affect several of them.
- "Launch the instances into a partition placement group ...": Three instances share each partition, and each partition [has its own set of racks](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-partition-separate-racks), so one rack failure can affect several instances of the same partition.
- "Launch the instances without a placement group, and ...": Without a group, Amazon EC2 tries to keep instances [spread out across the underlying hardware](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-optional-default-spread-out), but nothing guarantees distinct hardware for each instance.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The instances exchange data constantly, and the application needs low latency and high throughput between them" instead: a cluster placement group, for [low network latency, high network throughput, or both](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-placement-cluster-recommended-traffic-between-instances).

**Takeaway.** Separate hardware for a few critical instances means a spread placement group, not a cluster placement group.

**Review.** [A placement group decides whether instances sit close together or apart](2-deep.md#a-placement-group-decides-whether-instances-sit-close-together-or-apart-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 7

A company packages a nightly data export job as a container image. The job runs once each day. Each run is long-running and takes between 2 and 3 hours. The job needs no inbound network access. The operations team is small and prefers a serverless solution, so that nobody patches or scales instances for this job. Which compute options will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

- Package the job as an AWS Lambda function from the container image, and invoke the function once each day from an Amazon EventBridge schedule.
- Run the container image as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate, and start the task once each day from an Amazon EventBridge schedule.
- Run the container on an Amazon EC2 instance that runs all day, and start the job once each day from a cron entry on the instance.
- Submit the container image as a daily job to AWS Batch, with a compute environment that uses AWS Fargate resources.
- Deploy the container image to an AWS Elastic Beanstalk environment, and start the export each day from a scheduled task in the application code.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Run the container image as an Amazon ECS task on AWS Fargate, and start the task once each day from an Amazon EventBridge schedule.
- Submit the container image as a daily job to AWS Batch, with a compute environment that uses AWS Fargate resources.

**Deciding phrases.** "takes between 2 and 3 hours", "container image", "prefers a serverless solution", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Each run takes 2 to 3 hours, far longer than the [15 minutes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-timeout-15-minutes) that a Lambda function can run. Fargate runs the container with no instances to patch, and AWS Batch on Fargate also [automatically provisions compute resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-neighbour-batch-provisions-for-jobs) for each job.

- Fargate can [run containers without having to manage servers](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-fargate-no-servers-for-containers), and it suits [specific resource needs or persistent processes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-choose-fargate-containers-persistent) such as a long run.
- AWS Batch [automatically provisions compute resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-neighbour-batch-provisions-for-jobs) for each job and can use [Amazon EC2 instances, Fargate resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-neighbour-batch-runs-on-ec2-fargate), so with Fargate no instance is managed.

**Why not.**

- "Package the job as an AWS Lambda function ...": A Lambda function runs for at most [15 minutes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-timeout-15-minutes) per execution, so a run of 2 to 3 hours stops before it finishes.
- "Run the container on an Amazon EC2 instance ...": It works, but the team patches and scales the instance, an overhead that fits a need for [granular control over the compute environment](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-ec2-overhead-justified-for-control).
- "Deploy the container image to an AWS Elastic ...": Elastic Beanstalk is [specifically designed for running web applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-compute-guide-beanstalk-web-apps) on EC2 instances, so it adds instances to manage for a daily batch job.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each run takes about 2 minutes" instead: a scheduled Lambda function also fits, because a function can run up to [15 minutes](../facts/lambda.md#lambda-faq-timeout-15-minutes).

**Takeaway.** A container job that runs longer than a Lambda function can run fits Fargate or AWS Batch on Fargate.

**Review.** [An EC2 instance gives you control and you patch and scale it yourself](2-deep.md#an-ec2-instance-gives-you-control-and-you-patch-and-scale-it-yourself-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 8

A company runs a data processing job on Amazon EC2 instances every night to prepare reports. The job starts at 01:00, runs for about 3 hours on four instances of the same type, and the instances are not needed for the rest of the day. The job must not be interrupted and must finish before the business day starts. Which purchasing option is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Launch the instances as Spot Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.
- Launch the instances as On-Demand Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.
- Buy Standard Reserved Instances with a 3-year term and All Upfront payment for the instance type that the job uses.
- Launch the instances on Dedicated Hosts each night, and release the hosts after the job completes in the early morning.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Launch the instances as On-Demand Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.

**Deciding phrases.** "must not be interrupted", "about 3 hours", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The job has to run without interruption, which rules out Spot. AWS recommends On-Demand Instances for [short-term, irregular workloads that cannot be interrupted](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-on-demand-recommended-short-term-irregular). A [one-year or three-year commitment](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ri-term-one-or-three-years) suits steady use, not a job of about 3 hours a night.

**Why not.**

- "Launch the instances as Spot Instances each night, ...": [Spot Instances can be interrupted by Amazon EC2](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-only-difference-interruption-two-minutes) with [two minutes of notice](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-only-difference-interruption-two-minutes), and this job has to run without interruption.
- "Buy Standard Reserved Instances with a 3-year term ...": It works, but a Reserved Instance is a [one-year or three-year commitment](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ri-term-one-or-three-years) for one configuration, and the job uses its instances for about 3 hours a night.
- "Launch the instances on Dedicated Hosts each night, ...": Dedicated Hosts [help you address compliance requirements](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-purchasing-option-guidance) and server-bound licenses, and the stem names neither, so the hosts add cost.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The job can tolerate interruption and can restart from its last checkpoint" instead: Spot Instances, because AWS recommends Spot for [stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-recommended-stateless-fault-tolerant-flexible).

**Takeaway.** Work that has to finish without interruption runs on On-Demand, not Spot; a commitment pays off for steady use.

**Review.** [Spot Instances use spare capacity that EC2 can take back with two minutes notice](2-deep.md#spot-instances-use-spare-capacity-that-ec2-can-take-back-with-two-minutes-notice-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

### Question 9

A company runs a data processing job on Amazon EC2 instances every night to prepare reports. The job starts at 01:00, runs for about 3 hours on four instances of the same type, and the instances are not needed for the rest of the day. The job can tolerate interruption and can restart from its last checkpoint. Which purchasing option is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Launch the instances as Spot Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.
- Launch the instances as On-Demand Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.
- Buy Standard Reserved Instances with a 3-year term and All Upfront payment for the instance type that the job uses.
- Launch the instances on Dedicated Hosts each night, and release the hosts after the job completes in the early morning.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Launch the instances as Spot Instances each night, and terminate them after the job completes in the early morning.

**Deciding phrases.** "can tolerate interruption", "restart from its last checkpoint", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The job can tolerate interruption, so capacity that Amazon EC2 can take back fits. AWS recommends Spot for [stateless, fault-tolerant, flexible applications](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-recommended-stateless-fault-tolerant-flexible) and for teams that are [flexible about when your applications run](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-purchasing-option-guidance). The checkpoint limits the loss to the work after the last save.

**Why not.**

- "Launch the instances as On-Demand Instances each night, ...": On-Demand Instances work, but they cost more than Spot Instances, which run at a discount of [up to 90%](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-discount-up-to-90-percent) for work that can be interrupted.
- "Buy Standard Reserved Instances with a 3-year term ...": A Reserved Instance is a [one-year or three-year commitment](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ri-term-one-or-three-years) for instances that the job uses about 3 hours a night, so it costs more than Spot.
- "Launch the instances on Dedicated Hosts each night, ...": Dedicated Hosts [help you address compliance requirements](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-purchasing-option-guidance) and server-bound licenses, and the stem names neither, so the hosts add cost.

**Twin.** If the stem said "The job must not be interrupted and must finish before the business day starts" instead: On-Demand Instances, because [Spot Instances can be interrupted by Amazon EC2](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-only-difference-interruption-two-minutes).

**Takeaway.** A job that can restart from a checkpoint runs on Spot; a job that has to finish without interruption runs on On-Demand.

**Review.** [Spot Instances use spare capacity that EC2 can take back with two minutes notice](2-deep.md#spot-instances-use-spare-capacity-that-ec2-can-take-back-with-two-minutes-notice-5-min)

</details>

### Question 10

A company runs a mission-critical order-processing application on 8 Amazon EC2 instances of one instance type in one Availability Zone of an AWS Region. The company will keep the same instance family in the same Region for at least the next 3 years. The instances have steady-state usage all day, every day, and capacity is not a concern for the company. Which purchasing approach is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for 8 instances of the instance type in the Availability Zone where the instances run, with no end date.
- Buy a Compute Savings Plan with a 3-year term and an hourly commitment that covers the usage of the 8 instances in the Region.
- Buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan with a 3-year term for the instance family in the Region, sized for the 8 instances.
- Allocate Dedicated Hosts in the Availability Zone where the instances run, with enough capacity for the 8 instances, and launch the instances on the hosts.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Buy an EC2 Instance Savings Plan with a 3-year term for the instance family in the Region, sized for the 8 instances.

**Deciding phrases.** "steady-state usage all day, every day", "capacity is not a concern", "same instance family in the same Region", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The usage is steady, and the family and Region stay fixed, so the plan with the higher discount wins. Steady workloads [benefit most from long-term commitments through Savings Plans](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-steady-state-savings-plans), and EC2 Instance Savings Plans trade the flexibility of Compute Savings Plans for a higher discount on [a specific instance family within a Region](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility).

**Why not.**

- "Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for 8 instances ...": It works, but a reservation is [charged at the equivalent On-Demand rate](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-charged-used-or-not), so it adds no discount for steady usage.
- "Buy a Compute Savings Plan with a 3-year ...": It works, but Compute Savings Plans apply [regardless of Region, instance family, operating system](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-savings-plans-two-ec2-types-flexibility), and the company pays for that flexibility with a lower discount.
- "Allocate Dedicated Hosts in the Availability Zone where ...": It works, but each host is billed [regardless of the quantity or the size](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-billed-per-host-per-second) of its instances, which adds cost without a stated isolation need.

**Twin.** If the stem said "capacity for all 8 instances must always be available in that Availability Zone" instead: add a Capacity Reservation, and keep the plan, because [Savings Plans and Regional Reserved Instances apply](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-discount-from-sp-or-regional-ri) to it.

**Takeaway.** For steady usage in one family and Region, an EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives the larger Savings Plans discount.

**Review.** [On-Demand bills each second and a commitment lowers the price of steady use](2-deep.md#on-demand-bills-each-second-and-a-commitment-lowers-the-price-of-steady-use-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

## Extended

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q011 -->
### Question 11

A company runs Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. Administrators connect to the instances with SSH through a bastion host in a public subnet. A security review asks the company to restrict administrator access: the instances must have no inbound ports open, and the company wants to stop managing SSH keys. The instances run the SSM Agent and already reach the AWS service endpoints that they need. Which combination of steps will meet these requirements in the MOST secure way? (Select TWO.)

- Attach an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy to each instance through an instance profile.
- Keep the bastion host, and rotate the SSH keys on the bastion host and on the instances every 30 days.
- Remove the inbound SSH rules from the instance security groups, and connect to the instances with Session Manager.
- Store the access key of an IAM user on each instance so that the SSM Agent can call Systems Manager.
- Remove the bastion host, and allow inbound SSH on the instances from the IP address range of the office.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Attach an IAM role with the AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore managed policy to each instance through an instance profile.
- Remove the inbound SSH rules from the instance security groups, and connect to the instances with Session Manager.

**Deciding phrases.** "no inbound ports open", "stop managing SSH keys", "MOST secure"

**Why.** Session Manager meets both requirements. It gives a shell [without the need to open inbound ports](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-no-inbound-ports-bastion-keys) and with no SSH keys, and it connects when the instance role has the [AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-prereq-iam-role) policy. One step adds the role, and the other step removes the SSH rules.

- Session Manager connects when the instance has an attached IAM role with the [AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-prereq-iam-role) policy, and the role gives the agent temporary credentials.
- Session Manager works [without the need to open inbound ports](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-no-inbound-ports-bastion-keys), so the SSH rules and the bastion host are no longer needed.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the bastion host, and rotate the SSH ...": Rotation keeps the bastion host and the SSH keys, although Session Manager removes the need to [maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-no-inbound-ports-bastion-keys).
- "Store the access key of an IAM user ...": It works, but access keys [remain valid until you manually revoke them](../facts/iam.md#iam-long-term-keys-valid-until-revoked-temporary-expire), and the instance role already gives temporary credentials.
- "Remove the bastion host, and allow inbound SSH ...": A narrow source range still leaves the SSH port open and keeps the keys, although Session Manager works [without the need to open inbound ports](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-session-manager-no-inbound-ports-bastion-keys).

**Twin.** If the stem said "administrators must keep their own SSH clients, with no bastion host and no public IP addresses" instead: an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, which connects [without using a bastion host](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-eice-no-public-ip-no-igw-no-bastion).

**Takeaway.** No inbound port and no SSH keys means Session Manager plus an instance role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore.

**Review.** [A role gives the instance credentials and Session Manager needs no open port](2-deep.md#a-role-gives-the-instance-credentials-and-session-manager-needs-no-open-port-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q014 -->
### Question 12

A company launches its application instances in us-east-1 from a launch template that uses a custom AMI. The operations team builds a new AMI each month. For cross-Region disaster recovery, the company must be able to launch identical instances in us-west-2 within 1 hour if us-east-1 becomes unavailable. The same AWS account owns all resources in both Regions. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Add us-west-2 to the launch permissions of the AMI in us-east-1, so that instances in us-west-2 can launch from the same AMI.
- Reference the AMI ID from us-east-1 in a launch template in us-west-2, because one AMI ID is valid in every Region.
- Copy the AMI to us-west-2 after each monthly build, and reference the copied AMI in a launch template in us-west-2.
- Write a runbook that installs and configures the application on new instances in us-west-2 when a disaster occurs.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Copy the AMI to us-west-2 after each monthly build, and reference the copied AMI in a launch template in us-west-2.

**Deciding phrases.** "launch identical instances in us-west-2", "builds a new AMI each month", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** [AMIs are Region-specific resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-region-specific-copy), so an instance launches from an AMI in its own Region. A copy after each monthly build keeps an identical image ready in us-west-2, and a launch template there turns the copy into instances with one call.

**Why not.**

- "Add us-west-2 to the launch permissions of the ...": Launch permissions [determine who can use an AMI](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-launch-permissions-categories): [specific AWS accounts, organizations, or organizational units](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-launch-permissions-categories), not Regions.
- "Reference the AMI ID from us-east-1 in a ...": The us-east-1 AMI ID does not exist in us-west-2, because [AMIs are Region-specific resources](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-region-specific-copy).
- "Write a runbook that installs and configures the ...": It can work, but a manual build during a disaster is slow and error-prone, and it is more work than one AMI copy each month.

**Twin.** If the stem said "a second AWS account in us-east-1 must launch the instances" instead: share the AMI, because launch permissions name [specific AWS accounts, organizations, or organizational units](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-ami-launch-permissions-categories).

**Takeaway.** An AMI lives in one Region, so copy it to the recovery Region before a disaster.

**Review.** [An AMI and a launch template let you launch identical instances](2-deep.md#an-ami-and-a-launch-template-let-you-launch-identical-instances-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q018 -->
### Question 13

A company runs a batch workload that can tolerate interruption on Spot Instances. All instances use one instance type in one Availability Zone, and the request uses the lowest-price allocation strategy. Interruptions are frequent, and many jobs restart several times before they finish. The workload can run on many instance types and in any Availability Zone of the Region. The company wants fewer interruptions and wants to keep using Spot Instances. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Keep the lowest-price allocation strategy, because it picks the cheapest Spot capacity pools and so gives the lowest cost for the workload.
- Set a higher maximum Spot price in the request, so that Amazon EC2 interrupts the instances less often when the Spot price rises.
- Create separate Spot requests for several instance types in each Availability Zone, and route jobs by hand to the pools with fewer interruptions.
- Run the workload in an Auto Scaling group with many instance types across several Availability Zones and the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run the workload in an Auto Scaling group with many instance types across several Availability Zones and the price-capacity-optimized allocation strategy.

**Deciding phrases.** "one instance type in one Availability Zone", "lowest-price allocation strategy", "can run on many instance types", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Interruptions fall when Spot can choose from many pools. A Spot best practice is to be [flexible about which instance types you request](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-be-flexible-types-and-azs) and in which Availability Zones you deploy. AWS recommends launching Spot fleets [with Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-fleet-auto-scaling-recommended-method), and price-capacity-optimized picks the most available pools at a low price.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the lowest-price allocation strategy, because it picks ...": Lowest price has the [highest risk of interruption](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-fleet-spot-price-capacity-optimized-recommended), so keeping it leaves the frequent restarts in place.
- "Set a higher maximum Spot price in the ...": With a maximum price set, instances are [interrupted more frequently](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-max-price-more-interruptions) than without one, so a higher price does not protect them.
- "Create separate Spot requests for several instance types ...": It spreads the jobs across more pools, but many separate requests and routing by hand are more work than one Auto Scaling group.

**Twin.** If the stem said "each restart loses several hours of rendering work" instead: consider capacity-optimized, because it suits workloads with [a higher cost of interruption](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-capacity-optimized-high-restart-cost).

**Takeaway.** Fewer Spot interruptions come from many pools and price-capacity-optimized, not from a higher maximum price.

**Review.** [Spot Instances use spare capacity that EC2 can take back with two minutes notice](2-deep.md#spot-instances-use-spare-capacity-that-ec2-can-take-back-with-two-minutes-notice-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q020 -->
### Question 14

A company runs a license service on one Amazon EBS-backed EC2 instance. The instance is not in an Auto Scaling group and has no instance store volumes. Client applications connect to its Elastic IP address, and the license file is bound to the instance ID. The company must ensure that, after a failure of the underlying host hardware, the instance comes back with the same instance ID, private IP address, and Elastic IP address. The company wants to automate this. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

- Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the system status check of the instance, and set the alarm action to recover the instance.
- Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the system status check of the instance, and set the alarm action to reboot the instance.
- Register the instance with an Application Load Balancer, so that the load balancer replaces the instance when its health checks fail.
- Build an AWS Lambda function that stops and starts the instance, and invoke the function from an alarm on the system status check.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the system status check of the instance, and set the alarm action to recover the instance.

**Deciding phrases.** "failure of the underlying host hardware", "the same instance ID, private IP address, and Elastic IP address", "LEAST operational overhead"

**Why.** Host hardware problems fail the system status check, and those problems [require AWS involvement to repair](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-status-check-system-needs-aws). The recover action is [suited for System Health Check failures](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-alarm-reboot-instance-check-recover-system-check), and a recovered instance keeps its [private IP addresses, Elastic IP addresses](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-recovery-keeps-id-ips-metadata) and instance ID. On supported types, [simplified automatic recovery is enabled during instance launch](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-recovery-simplified-enabled-by-default); of these options, the alarm is the recovery that you configure and control.

**Why not.**

- "Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm on the system ...": The reboot action is [recommended for Instance Health Check failures](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-alarm-reboot-instance-check-recover-system-check), and after a reboot [the instance remains on the same host computer](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-reboot-same-host-keeps-data) that failed.
- "Register the instance with an Application Load Balancer, ...": When a target fails its checks, [it stops routing traffic to that target](../facts/elb.md#elb-unhealthy-target-stop-resume); the load balancer launches no replacement and restores no instance.
- "Build an AWS Lambda function that stops and ...": It can work, because you can [stop and start the instance yourself](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-status-check-system-needs-aws), but the function is custom code to maintain, and the recover action is built in.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the instance status check fails because the operating system runs out of memory" instead: the reboot action, because it is [recommended for Instance Health Check failures](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-alarm-reboot-instance-check-recover-system-check).

**Takeaway.** A failed system status check is a host problem; the recover action keeps the instance ID and addresses.

**Review.** [Recovery and a moved network interface keep an instances addresses after a failure](2-deep.md#recovery-and-a-moved-network-interface-keep-an-instances-addresses-after-a-failure-5-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q013 -->
### Question 15

A company runs a production web application on Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. The production application must be highly available and must keep serving users if one Availability Zone fails. The company also runs a development copy of the application that engineers use only during office hours on weekdays. A short outage of the development environment is acceptable. Which combination of steps is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

- Run the production instances in two or more Availability Zones of the Region behind an Application Load Balancer.
- Run the production instances on larger instance types in one Availability Zone behind an Application Load Balancer.
- Run the development instances in one Availability Zone, and stop them outside office hours and on weekends.
- Run the development instances in three Availability Zones, and hold their capacity with On-Demand Capacity Reservations.
- Run the production application in two AWS Regions, with active instances in both Regions at all times.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.**

- Run the production instances in two or more Availability Zones of the Region behind an Application Load Balancer.
- Run the development instances in one Availability Zone, and stop them outside office hours and on weekends.

**Deciding phrases.** "must keep serving users if one Availability Zone fails", "A short outage of the development environment is acceptable", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The two environments need different availability. Production has to survive a zone failure, so it runs [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) behind the load balancer. Development accepts an outage, so one zone and stops after office hours cut its cost by [70% or more](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-wa-turn-off-after-hours-70-percent).

- Instances [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) survive [the failure of a single location](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) in the Region.
- You can [save money by deploying your resources in only one Availability Zone](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-dev-test-one-az-saves-money) for development, and turning instances off after hours saves [70% or more](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-wa-turn-off-after-hours-70-percent).

**Why not.**

- "Run the production instances on larger instance types ...": All the instances stop serving if their one zone fails, and a load balancer does not change that; production needs instances [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure).
- "Run the development instances in three Availability Zones, ...": Development accepts an outage, so three zones add cost, and a reservation is [charged at the equivalent On-Demand rate](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-capacity-reservation-charged-used-or-not) even when nothing runs in it.
- "Run the production application in two AWS Regions, ...": A second Region adds cost that the stem does not ask for, because instances [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) already survive a zone failure.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the development environment also has to survive a zone failure" instead: run development [across multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-bp-multi-az-critical-components) as well.

**Takeaway.** Match availability to the workload class: production in several zones, development in one zone and stopped after hours.

**Review.** [Instances in several Availability Zones survive the failure of one zone](2-deep.md#instances-in-several-availability-zones-survive-the-failure-of-one-zone-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q017 -->
### Question 16

A company plans to migrate Microsoft SQL Server databases from its data center to Amazon EC2. The company owns SQL Server licenses that it is allowed to bring to AWS. The license terms count physical cores, and the vendor requires the company to report the number of sockets and physical cores that the software runs on. The databases run all day, every day. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Launch the database instances as Dedicated Instances, and bring the existing SQL Server licenses to the instances.
- Launch the database instances on Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts, and bring the existing SQL Server licenses to the hosts.
- Launch the database instances with shared tenancy from AMIs that include the SQL Server license in the hourly price.
- Launch the database instances as Spot Instances with shared tenancy, and bring the existing SQL Server licenses to them.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Launch the database instances on Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts, and bring the existing SQL Server licenses to the hosts.

**Deciding phrases.** "count physical cores", "report the number of sockets and physical cores", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** Licenses that count physical cores need a server whose cores the company can see. Dedicated Hosts give [comprehensive Bring Your Own License (BYOL) support](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-byol-per-socket-core) and show [the number of sockets and physical cores](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-socket-core-visibility). With its own SQL Server licenses, the company pays [no additional charge for software usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-byol-no-software-charge).

**Why not.**

- "Launch the database instances as Dedicated Instances, and ...": Dedicated Instances give [no visibility](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-socket-core-visibility) of sockets and physical cores, so the company cannot report them to the vendor.
- "Launch the database instances with shared tenancy from ...": License-included AMIs work, but the company pays for SQL Server again, although its own licenses on Dedicated Hosts bring [no additional charge for software usage](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-dedicated-host-byol-no-software-charge).
- "Launch the database instances as Spot Instances with ...": Spot Instances do not suit workloads that are [inflexible, stateful, fault-intolerant, or tightly coupled](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-spot-not-suitable-stateful-inflexible), and shared tenancy shows no sockets or cores.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the company has no SQL Server licenses of its own" instead: license-included AMIs on shared tenancy fit, because there is no license to bring to a Dedicated Host.

**Takeaway.** Licenses that count sockets or physical cores point to Dedicated Hosts, not Dedicated Instances.

**Review.** [Only a reservation holds capacity and a Dedicated Host holds a whole server](2-deep.md#only-a-reservation-holds-capacity-and-a-dedicated-host-holds-a-whole-server-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q019 -->
### Question 17

A company runs an internal API for its order system on one Amazon EC2 T3 instance in unlimited mode. The load is steady-state: average CPU utilization stays at about 80% all day, every day, far above the baseline of the instance. Each monthly bill includes charges for surplus CPU credits. The API must keep its current performance. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Keep the T3 instance in unlimited mode, because the hourly price of the instance covers CPU bursts of any length.
- Change the T3 instance to standard mode so that the instance stops accruing surplus credit charges each month.
- Move the API to a general purpose M instance or a compute optimized C instance with a similar number of vCPUs.
- Run the API on a T3 Spot Instance in unlimited mode, and launch a new Spot Instance after each interruption.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Move the API to a general purpose M instance or a compute optimized C instance with a similar number of vCPUs.

**Deciding phrases.** "steady-state", "about 80% all day", "must keep its current performance", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** A steady load far above the baseline decides it. AWS suggests M or C instances when workloads [consistently require CPU usage much higher](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-burstable-sustained-high-cpu-use-m-or-c) than the baseline. In unlimited mode, an average above the baseline across a [rolling 24-hour period](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-unlimited-24-hour-baseline-rule) adds a [flat additional rate per vCPU-hour](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-unlimited-24-hour-baseline-rule).

**Why not.**

- "Keep the T3 instance in unlimited mode, because ...": The hourly price covers spikes when the average stays at or below the baseline across a [rolling 24-hour period](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-unlimited-24-hour-baseline-rule); above it, AWS bills a [flat additional rate per vCPU-hour](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-unlimited-24-hour-baseline-rule).
- "Change the T3 instance to standard mode so ...": In standard mode, an instance with no credits left [gradually comes down to baseline CPU utilization](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-no-credits-down-to-baseline) and [cannot burst above baseline](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-no-credits-down-to-baseline) until it earns more credits, so a steady load near 80% loses performance.
- "Run the API on a T3 Spot Instance ...": AWS recommends that you [launch your T4g or T3 Spot Instances in standard mode to avoid paying higher costs](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-spot-standard-mode-recommended), and interruptions break the steady API.

**Twin.** If the stem said "CPU stays near 5% with short peaks each morning" instead: keep a burstable T instance, because it earns credits when it [stays below the CPU baseline](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-burstable-standard-earn-spend-credits).

**Takeaway.** Steady CPU far above the baseline belongs on M or C instances; burstable instances fit low averages with short peaks.

**Review.** [A burstable instance earns CPU credits while idle and spends them in peaks](2-deep.md#a-burstable-instance-earns-cpu-credits-while-idle-and-spends-them-in-peaks-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->

<!-- quiz:start id=ec2-q021 -->
### Question 18

A company runs a nightly analytics job on a cluster of Amazon EC2 instances in one AWS Region. The nodes exchange several terabytes of data with each other during each run. The job can tolerate interruption, and a delay of one day is acceptable if an Availability Zone fails, because the cluster can be rebuilt from scratch. The nodes now run in three Availability Zones, and the data transfer charges are high. Which change is the MOST cost-effective way to meet these requirements?

- Keep the nodes in three Availability Zones, and add nodes in each zone so that the cluster stays highly available.
- Assign an Elastic IP address to each node, and send the traffic between the nodes to the Elastic IP addresses.
- Move half of the nodes to a second AWS Region, and send the traffic between the two halves over the AWS network.
- Run all the nodes in one Availability Zone, and launch them into a cluster placement group in that zone.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**Answer.** Run all the nodes in one Availability Zone, and launch them into a cluster placement group in that zone.

**Deciding phrases.** "exchange several terabytes of data with each other", "a delay of one day is acceptable", "run in three Availability Zones", "MOST cost-effective"

**Why.** The cost comes from traffic between zones: each instance is [charged for its data in and data out](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-cross-az-transfer-charged-both-sides) when the other node sits in another zone. Data transfer [within the same Availability Zone is free](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-data-transfer-same-az-free-cross-az-charged). The stem accepts a delay of a day after a zone failure, so one zone is enough.

**Why not.**

- "Keep the nodes in three Availability Zones, and ...": Three zones keep the traffic between zones, and [charges apply for cross-Availability Zone communication](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-data-transfer-same-az-free-cross-az-charged), although the stem accepts a delay after a zone failure.
- "Assign an Elastic IP address to each node, ...": Rates apply when public or Elastic IP addresses are used, in any zone, and the company is [only charged once for a given instance](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-faq-regional-transfer-charged-once): the Elastic IP addresses keep the charge.
- "Move half of the nodes to a second ...": Traffic between Regions brings [a charge for data transfer across Regions](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-data-transfer-cross-region-charged), so splitting the cluster adds cost instead of removing it.

**Twin.** If the stem said "the results are needed every morning, even if an Availability Zone fails" instead: keep several zones and pay for the transfer, because instances [in multiple Availability Zones](../facts/ec2.md#ec2-multi-az-protects-from-location-failure) survive a zone failure.

**Takeaway.** Traffic between zones costs money; a job that accepts a zone outage can save that cost by running in one zone.

**Review.** [Instances in several Availability Zones survive the failure of one zone](2-deep.md#instances-in-several-availability-zones-survive-the-failure-of-one-zone-4-min)

</details>
<!-- quiz:end -->
